# Medical billing staff for US practices, without the hiring headache

URL: https://medicalbillingteam.com/

Claims pile up when one person is out. Denials sit unworked. Prior authorizations eat your front desk's afternoon. This site explains how practices and billing companies solve those problems, including when a dedicated remote billing team makes sense and when it doesn't.

**Get a free staffing assessment.** Tell us a little about your practice and a billing staffing specialist will follow up. It takes about a minute.


## Who this site helps

- **Solo and small practices** where the office manager is also the biller, the scheduler and the person who calls payers.
- **Specialty groups** such as behavioral health, physical therapy, chiropractic, labs and ambulatory surgery centers (ASCs), where payer rules and authorizations are specialty-specific.
- **Multi-location groups** that need consistent billing processes across sites.
- **Practice and billing managers** who need more hands on the A/R, denial or authorization queues without adding local headcount.
- **Medical billing companies** that need to add trained staff as they win new clients.


## Common billing problems we write about

- **Denials that never get reworked.** In a vendor survey of billing professionals, 40% reported an increase in denials over the prior year ([Tebra, 2025](https://www.tebra.com/theintake/getting-paid/medical-billing-pain-points-insights-solutions)). Federal transparency data show HealthCare.gov insurers denied 20% of in-network claims in 2023 ([KFF](https://www.kff.org/private-insurance/claims-denials-and-appeals-in-aca-marketplace-plans-in-2023/)).
- **Aging A/R.** Claims nobody has followed up on after 30, 60 or 90 days.
- **Prior authorization workload.** Physicians surveyed by the AMA reported an average of 39 prior authorization requests per physician per week, taking about 13 hours of physician and staff time ([AMA](https://www.ama-assn.org/practice-management/prior-authorization/fixing-prior-auth-nearly-40-prior-authorizations-week-way)).
- **Eligibility surprises.** Coverage changes discovered after the visit, not before.
- **Hiring and turnover.** In the same vendor survey, 38% of billers said they struggle to find qualified candidates ([Tebra, 2025](https://www.tebra.com/theintake/getting-paid/medical-billing-pain-points-insights-solutions)).

Read more: [Revenue cycle management staffing](/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/) · [Denial management](/denial-management/) · [How to reduce AR days](/reduce-ar-days/)


## The remote billing team model, explained

A remote billing team is not a software product and not a full billing takeover. It is dedicated people working your queues:

- **They work in your systems.** Your practice management system, clearinghouse and payer portals, with access you grant and can revoke.
- **They follow your rules.** Your fee schedules, your write-off policy, your escalation path.
- **They are dedicated.** The same people every day, so they learn your payers and your providers.
- **You keep control.** You own the process and the payer relationships. The staffing provider recruits, employs, trains and supports the staff.

Typical roles include billing specialists, A/R follow-up specialists, eligibility and benefits verification (VOB) staff, prior authorization coordinators, payment posters, denial follow-up specialists and admissions or intake support.

This site is operated by [Alliance Global Solutions](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/), which provides remote staff from the Philippines. We think a staffing model fits some practices well and others not at all. Our [cost guide](/medical-billing-staffing-cost/) compares in-house, outsourced and remote options side by side.


## HIPAA comes first



If anyone outside your practice will touch patient data, HIPAA is the first question, not the last. Before remote or offshore billing staff log in to anything, you should expect:

- **A business associate agreement (BAA)** with the agency, because a company that handles billing involving protected health information on your behalf is a business associate under HIPAA ([HHS](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/guidance/business-associates/index.html)).
- **Minimum necessary, role-based access.** Staff see only what their job requires.
- **Strong access controls:** unique logins, multi-factor authentication, secure remote access (VPN or virtual desktop) and no local downloads or printing.
- **Documented training, risk analysis and a breach-reporting process.**

One more thing to know: **there is no official "HIPAA certification"** for companies or staff. HHS's Office for Civil Rights states that it does not endorse, certify or recommend specific technology or products ([HHS](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/special-topics/health-information-technology/cloud-computing/index.html)). Be cautious of anyone who claims to be "HIPAA certified."

[Read the full HIPAA guide for outsourced and offshore billing staff →](/hipaa-outsourced-medical-billing/)

## Short FAQ

**What is a remote medical billing team?**
Dedicated billing and RCM staff who work remotely in your systems and under your workflows. You direct the work; the staffing provider handles recruiting, employment and support.

**Is this the same as hiring a billing company?**
No. A billing company usually takes over the whole function. A staffing model gives you dedicated people and you keep control.

**What does the free assessment involve?**
A short conversation about your workload and gaps. No obligation, and no patient information needed.

**Can remote staff work within HIPAA?**
Yes, when the right agreements and safeguards are in place. There is no official HIPAA certification, so ask about the specific safeguards instead. See the [HIPAA guide](/hipaa-outsourced-medical-billing/).

[More questions →](/faq/)

## FAQ

**What is a remote medical billing team?**
It is one or more dedicated billing and revenue cycle staff who work remotely inside your systems, under your workflows, doing tasks such as eligibility checks, prior authorizations, claim follow-up, payment posting and denial work. You direct the work; a staffing provider handles recruiting, employment and supervision support.

**Is this the same as outsourcing my billing to a billing company?**
Not exactly. A billing company usually takes over the whole function, often for a percentage of collections. A staffing model gives you dedicated people who work your queues in your software, and you keep control of the process and your payer relationships.

**What does the free staffing assessment involve?**
A short call about your workload, specialty, current setup and gaps. We discuss which roles, if any, would make sense. There is no obligation, and we never need patient information for this conversation.

**Do you need patient information to give me an assessment?**
No. Please do not include any patient information in forms, emails or chat. Practice-level details, such as specialty, number of providers and a collections range, are enough.

**Can remote staff work with HIPAA requirements?**
Remote staff can work within HIPAA's rules when the right contracts and safeguards are in place, including a business associate agreement, role-based access and training. There is no official 'HIPAA certification' for any company or person. See our HIPAA guide for the questions to ask.

# Revenue cycle management staffing: roles, workflow, KPIs and costs

URL: https://medicalbillingteam.com/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/

*Last reviewed: October 18, 2026.*

Revenue cycle management (RCM) is every step between a patient booking an appointment and your practice collecting the last dollar for that visit. When one step is understaffed, the effect shows up later, as denials, aging A/R and write-offs. This guide covers the RCM workflow, the roles behind it, the KPIs worth tracking and the three main ways practices and billing companies staff it: in-house, outsourced and dedicated remote or offshore teams.


## What RCM staffing means

RCM staffing is the work of putting trained people on each part of the revenue cycle. For a solo practice, that might be one person juggling everything. For a multi-location group or a billing company, it is a team with defined queues: eligibility, authorizations, coding, charge entry, claims, denials, A/R and posting.

There are three common models:

1. **In-house staff.** You recruit, employ, train and manage billing staff locally.
2. **Outsourced RCM.** A billing or RCM company takes over the function, typically under a contract priced as a percentage of collections or per claim. You trade control for convenience.
3. **Dedicated remote or offshore RCM staff.** A staffing provider recruits and employs staff, often in another country, who work full time in *your* systems and follow *your* processes. You keep control of the workflow and payer relationships.

Many organizations mix models, for example keeping a local billing manager and coder while adding remote staff for eligibility, posting and A/R follow-up.


## The RCM workflow, step by step

### 1. Eligibility and benefits verification

Before the visit, staff confirm active coverage, plan type, copays, deductibles, coordination of benefits and whether a referral or authorization is required. Errors here cause problems later: in a 2025 vendor survey of billing professionals, coordination of benefits issues were the most commonly cited denial reason (45% of respondents), followed by non-coverage (39%) ([Tebra](https://www.tebra.com/theintake/getting-paid/medical-billing-pain-points-insights-solutions)). Read more in our [eligibility verification and prior authorization guide](/eligibility-verification-prior-authorization/).

### 2. Prior authorization

Staff submit and track authorization requests, attach clinical documentation and follow up on pending decisions. The AMA's survey of 1,000 physicians found practices complete an average of 39 prior authorization requests per physician per week, and that 40% of physicians have staff who work exclusively on prior authorizations ([AMA](https://www.ama-assn.org/practice-management/prior-authorization/fixing-prior-auth-nearly-40-prior-authorizations-week-way)). Under the CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization final rule, impacted payers (Medicare Advantage, Medicaid and CHIP fee-for-service and managed care; FFE qualified health plans are excluded from this particular timeframe requirement) must send decisions within 72 hours for expedited requests and seven calendar days for standard requests, starting in 2026, and must give a specific reason for denials ([CMS](https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/cms-interoperability-and-prior-authorization-final-rule-cms-0057-f)).

### 3. Medical coding

Certified coders assign CPT, HCPCS and ICD-10-CM codes from provider documentation. Code sets change on a schedule: ICD-10-CM updates generally take effect October 1 each year ([CMS](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/coding-billing/icd-10-codes)), and the AMA's CPT Editorial Panel maintains CPT ([AMA](https://www.ama-assn.org/practice-management/cpt/cpt-overview-and-code-approval)). Coding is skilled work; remote coders should hold recognized credentials and specialty experience.

### 4. Charge entry

Charges, modifiers, units, place of service and rendering provider are entered into the practice management system, often with a charge review step to catch missing documentation or mismatched codes before claims go out.

### 5. Claims submission and scrubbing

Claims are scrubbed for errors, submitted through a clearinghouse, and rejections (claims the payer or clearinghouse never accepted) are corrected quickly. Timely filing limits matter: Medicare generally requires claims within one calendar year of the date of service ([CMS Medicare Claims Processing Manual, Ch. 1, §70](https://www.cms.gov/regulations-and-guidance/guidance/manuals/downloads/clm104c01.pdf)), and commercial payer limits are often shorter.

### 6. Denial management

Denied claims are categorized by reason, corrected, resubmitted or appealed, and the root cause is fed back to the front end. HealthCare.gov insurers denied 20% of in-network claims in 2023 according to KFF's analysis of federal data, and consumers appealed fewer than 1% of denied claims ([KFF](https://www.kff.org/private-insurance/claims-denials-and-appeals-in-aca-marketplace-plans-in-2023/)). That data covers one market segment, but it shows why someone needs to own the denial queue. See [denial management basics](/denial-management/).

### 7. A/R follow-up

A/R specialists work unpaid claims by age and dollar value, check status on payer portals, call payers and escalate. The goal is to resolve claims before they age past timely filing or appeal limits. See [how to reduce AR days](/reduce-ar-days/).

### 8. Payment posting

Payments from ERAs (835 files), paper EOBs, lockbox deposits and patient payments are posted and reconciled to the bank. Accurate posting is how you spot underpayments, incorrect adjustments and denials that arrive inside a "paid" remittance.

### Supporting functions

- **Credentialing and payer enrollment**, so providers can bill payers at all.
- **Patient statements and patient A/R.**
- **Reporting**, so the practice sees the KPIs below every month.


## RCM roles you can staff

| Role | What they do | Remote-friendly? |
|---|---|---|
| Eligibility / VOB specialist | Verifies coverage and benefits before visits | Yes |
| Prior authorization coordinator | Submits and tracks authorizations | Yes |
| Medical coder | Assigns CPT/HCPCS/ICD-10 codes | Yes, with credentials |
| Charge entry specialist | Enters and reviews charges | Yes |
| Billing / claims specialist | Scrubs and submits claims, works rejections | Yes |
| Denial management specialist | Works denials and appeals | Yes |
| A/R follow-up specialist | Works unpaid claims, calls payers | Yes |
| Payment poster | Posts and reconciles payments | Yes |
| Credentialing specialist | Manages enrollment and re-credentialing | Yes |
| Billing manager | Owns process, reporting and escalation | Often local |


## RCM KPIs, defined

Definitions vary slightly between organizations. Pick one definition, document it, and use it consistently.

- **Days in A/R:** total accounts receivable divided by average daily charges (for example, total charges over the last 90 days divided by 90). It estimates how long, on average, it takes to collect.
- **Clean claim rate:** the share of claims accepted and processed on first submission without edits, rejections or requests for more information.
- **Denial rate:** denied claims (or denied dollars) divided by total claims (or dollars) submitted in a period. Track by payer and reason code.
- **Net collection rate:** payments collected divided by the amount you were contractually entitled to collect (charges minus contractual adjustments) for the period. It shows how much collectible revenue you actually captured.
- **First-pass resolution rate:** the share of claims paid in full, or otherwise fully resolved, after the first submission with no further touches.
- **A/R over 90 (or 120) days:** the share of A/R older than 90 or 120 days.

**About benchmarks:** published benchmarks vary widely by specialty, payer mix and methodology, and many come from member-only surveys or vendor marketing. We don't publish a benchmark number unless we can cite a public source. Instead, trend your own numbers monthly and compare with specialty data you trust. The [Medical Billing Health Checklist](/checklist/) includes a simple KPI worksheet.


## In-house vs outsourced vs dedicated remote RCM: how to compare costs

We won't give you invented price ranges. Here is how to build a fair comparison with your own numbers.

**In-house cost** is more than salary. Add wages, payroll taxes, benefits, paid leave, recruiting, training, software seats, equipment, workspace and management time. Public data help as a starting point: the BLS reports a May 2025 median hourly wage of $23.32 for billing and posting clerks ([BLS OEWS](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/ocwage.t01.htm)) and a median annual wage of $51,140 for medical records specialists, the BLS category that includes medical coders ([BLS OOH](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/medical-records-and-health-information-technicians.htm)). Benefits add materially on top: in private industry, benefits averaged 30.0% of employer compensation costs in June 2026 ([BLS ECEC](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/ecec.nr0.htm)). Then add the cost of vacancies, because unworked queues keep aging while you hire.

**Outsourced RCM cost** is usually a percentage of collections, a per-claim fee, or a hybrid. Ask what is included (coding? credentialing? patient statements? appeals?), how "collections" is defined, minimums, setup fees and exit terms. Model the fee against your actual monthly collections.

**Dedicated remote or offshore staff** are usually priced per full-time staff member per month or per hour. Compare that rate against fully loaded in-house cost for the same role, then add your own costs: management time, onboarding, software seats and secure remote access (for example, a VDI setup).

**Non-cost factors** matter as much as price: control of the workflow, visibility into queues, turnover risk, coverage during absences, HIPAA safeguards, and how quickly you can add or remove capacity. Our [medical billing staffing cost guide](/medical-billing-staffing-cost/) walks through a worksheet.


## Choosing an RCM staffing partner

Whatever model you pick, ask:

- Which roles can you staff, and what is the experience level for my specialty?
- Will staff be dedicated to us, and who supervises them day to day?
- How do you handle HIPAA: BAA, access controls, training, incident response? (See our [HIPAA guide](/hipaa-outsourced-medical-billing/).)
- How will we measure performance, and what reporting do we get?
- What happens if a staff member leaves?
- What are the contract length, notice period and exit terms?

Be wary of any vendor that guarantees a specific reduction in denials or A/R days before seeing your data. Results depend on your payers, specialty, documentation and starting point.


## Where a remote RCM team fits

A dedicated remote team tends to fit when you have steady, queue-based work (eligibility, posting, A/R, denials), systems that support secure remote access, and someone in-house who can own the process. It fits less well if your processes are undocumented or your billing system can't support remote access securely.

This site is operated by [Alliance Global Solutions](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/), which provides remote staff from the Philippines; you can see the company's broader [outsourcing services](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/services/) on its own site. If you'd like a second opinion on your RCM staffing, request a [free staffing assessment](/contact/).


## FAQ

**What is revenue cycle management staffing?**
Filling the roles that move an encounter from scheduling to payment: eligibility, authorization, coding, charge entry, claims, denials, A/R and posting.

**What is the difference between outsourced RCM and an offshore RCM team?**
Outsourced RCM hands the function to a vendor. An offshore RCM team is dedicated staff abroad working your queues under your direction.

**Which RCM KPIs should a small practice track first?**
Days in A/R, denial rate, clean claim rate and net collection rate.

**Is there a standard benchmark for days in A/R?**
Benchmarks vary by specialty and source. Trend your own numbers and compare with specialty data you trust.

**Can remote RCM staff do medical coding?**
Yes, with the right credentials and specialty experience. Test before live coding.

## FAQ

**What is revenue cycle management staffing?**
It means filling the roles that move a patient encounter from scheduling to final payment: eligibility and benefits verification, prior authorization, coding, charge entry, claim submission, denial management, A/R follow-up and payment posting. You can staff these roles in-house, outsource the whole function, or add dedicated remote or offshore staff who work in your systems.

**What is the difference between outsourced RCM and an offshore RCM team?**
Outsourced RCM usually means a vendor runs the revenue cycle for you, often for a percentage of collections. An offshore RCM team is a staffing arrangement where dedicated staff abroad work your queues under your direction. Some vendors combine both.

**Which RCM KPIs should a small practice track first?**
Start with days in A/R, denial rate, clean claim rate and net collection rate. They are straightforward to calculate from most practice management systems and show where the cycle is slowing.

**Is there a standard benchmark for days in A/R?**
Benchmarks vary by specialty, payer mix and data source, and many industry benchmark reports are member-only. Track your own trend month to month and compare with specialty-specific data from sources you trust, rather than relying on a single generic number.

**Can remote RCM staff do medical coding?**
Yes, if they hold the right credentials and specialty experience. Coding is a skilled role; ask for certification details and test candidates on your specialty's documentation before they code live claims.

# Denial management basics: a practical guide for practices and billing teams

URL: https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-management/

*Last reviewed: October 18, 2026.*

Every practice gets denials. The difference between practices that lose revenue to them and practices that don't is usually not software. It's whether someone owns the denial queue, works it on a schedule and fixes the causes upstream. This guide covers the basics and where staffing fits in. It is part of our [revenue cycle management staffing](/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/) series.


## Why denials deserve a dedicated owner

Public data show how common denials are. KFF's analysis of federal transparency data found HealthCare.gov insurers denied 20% of in-network claims in 2023 ([KFF](https://www.kff.org/private-insurance/claims-denials-and-appeals-in-aca-marketplace-plans-in-2023/)). That covers one market segment, but the pattern is familiar to anyone who works claims. In a 2025 vendor survey of billing professionals, 40% reported that denials had increased over the previous year ([Tebra](https://www.tebra.com/theintake/getting-paid/medical-billing-pain-points-insights-solutions)).

When nobody owns denials, they age quietly in a work queue until the appeal window closes.


## Rejections vs denials

- **Rejection:** the claim never entered the payer's adjudication system, usually because of a data or formatting error (wrong member ID format, missing NPI, invalid code). Fix and resubmit quickly. Rejections don't usually carry appeal rights because no decision was made.
- **Denial:** the payer processed the claim and refused payment in whole or part. The remittance carries claim adjustment reason codes (CARCs) and often remittance advice remark codes (RARCs) explaining why. These are standard code sets used by all payers, as CMS describes in its Medicare Claims Processing Manual ([CMS, Ch. 1](https://www.cms.gov/regulations-and-guidance/guidance/manuals/downloads/clm104c01.pdf)).


## Common root causes

The same vendor survey asked billers about top denial reasons ([Tebra](https://www.tebra.com/theintake/getting-paid/medical-billing-pain-points-insights-solutions)):

- coordination of benefits issues (45% of respondents);
- non-coverage (39%);
- prior authorization and referral issues (31%);
- timely filing errors (26%);
- inaccurate patient demographic information (25%).

In KFF's federal data, insurers cited administrative reasons for 21% of in-network denials and lack of prior authorization or referral for 9%, while the largest category was "Other" at 34% ([KFF](https://www.kff.org/private-insurance/claims-denials-and-appeals-in-aca-marketplace-plans-in-2023/)).

Most of these trace back to the **front end**: eligibility checks, demographics capture and authorizations. That's why denial management and [eligibility and prior authorization](/eligibility-verification-prior-authorization/) work belong together.


## A simple denial workflow

### 1. Capture every denial

Make sure denials from ERAs (835s), paper EOBs and payer portals all land in one queue. Payment posters are often the first to see a denial; they should flag it, not just post a zero.

### 2. Categorize

Tag each denial by payer, reason code group (eligibility, authorization, coding, timely filing, medical necessity, duplicate, bundling, other) and whether it is **preventable**.

### 3. Prioritize

Sort by appeal or corrected-claim deadline first, then dollar value. A small denial with a deadline next week beats a large one with three months left.

### 4. Act

- **Correct and resubmit** for fixable data errors (demographics, codes, modifiers).
- **Appeal** when the claim was correct and the payer was wrong. Use the payer's form, cite the policy, attach documentation, and track the appeal date.
- **Bill the right party** for coordination of benefits issues.
- **Write off** only under your written write-off policy, with approval.

### 5. Track and close the loop

Log the outcome. Each month, review the top preventable reasons by payer and send fixes upstream: a front-desk script change, an authorization rule, a coding education note.


## Appeals: the basics

- Read the denial reason and the payer's policy before writing anything.
- Know the deadline. Payer appeal windows differ, and Medicare has its own multi-level appeals process.
- Include what the payer needs: claim details, the specific reason you disagree, policy citations and supporting documentation.
- Follow up. An appeal that's never tracked is an appeal that's lost.

Appeals can succeed. KFF reports that among Medicare Advantage prior authorization denials in 2023 that were appealed, 81.7% were fully or partially overturned, yet only 11.7% of denials were appealed (cited in [AMA](https://www.ama-assn.org/practice-management/prior-authorization/fixing-prior-auth-nearly-40-prior-authorizations-week-way)). That's prior authorization data, not claims, but it shows the value of persistence.


## Denial KPIs to track

- **Denial rate:** denied claims (or dollars) ÷ claims (or dollars) submitted, by payer and reason.
- **Preventable denial share:** denials in categories the practice controls.
- **Days to work a denial:** from receipt to first action.
- **Overturn rate:** successful appeals ÷ appeals filed.
- **Denial write-offs:** dollars written off due to denials, per month.

We don't publish a universal "good" denial rate, because public benchmarks vary by specialty and methodology. Trend your own numbers. Our [RCM KPI definitions](/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/) explain how to calculate each one consistently.


## Who should do denial work?

Denial work needs someone with payer knowledge, coding familiarity, patience on the phone and protected time. Options:

- **Your existing biller**, if they actually have the hours. Often they don't.
- **A dedicated denial management specialist**, in-house or remote, who works the queue daily.
- **An outsourced billing company** that includes appeals in its scope (confirm this; some don't).

A remote denial specialist works in your billing system and payer portals under your rules and write-off policy. If you're considering that route, read our [guide to hiring remote medical billers](/hire-remote-medical-billers/) and make sure HIPAA safeguards are in place first ([HIPAA guide](/hipaa-outsourced-medical-billing/)).


## Preventing denials upstream

- Verify eligibility and benefits before every visit, not just new patients.
- Confirm authorization requirements by payer and service, and track expirations and visit limits.
- Capture demographics and insurance cards accurately; re-verify at every visit.
- Scrub claims before submission and fix rejections daily.
- Give coders feedback on recurring coding denials.
- Track timely filing deadlines per payer.

This site is operated by [Alliance Global Solutions](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/), a provider of remote billing staff. If your denial queue is growing faster than your team can work it, you can [contact the company directly](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/contact/) or request a [free staffing assessment](/contact/) here.


## A weekly denial routine for small teams

If you only have a few hours a week for denials, a fixed routine keeps them from piling up:

1. **Monday:** pull new denials from ERAs and the clearinghouse into one list. Tag each by payer, reason code and dollar amount.
2. **Tuesday-Wednesday:** correct and resubmit the quick fixes (demographics, coding errors, missing modifiers) and call payers on the unclear ones.
3. **Thursday:** draft appeals for high-dollar or recurring denials, with supporting documentation and the payer's appeal deadline noted.
4. **Friday:** review the week. What were the top three reasons? Which could the front desk, providers or coders prevent? Send one short note to the people who can fix the cause.

Keep the list in a shared tracker so nothing depends on one person's memory.


## FAQ

**What is the difference between a rejection and a denial?**
A rejection was never accepted for processing; a denial was processed and not paid. Fix and resubmit rejections; correct, resubmit or appeal denials.

**What are the most common causes of denials?**
Eligibility and coordination of benefits, non-covered services, missing authorizations, timely filing, coding errors and demographics.

**How often should denials be worked?**
Daily or weekly, by deadline and dollar value.

**What is a good denial rate?**
It varies by specialty and method. Trend your own rate by payer and reason.

**Should denial work be in-house or outsourced?**
Either works if one person owns the queue and feeds root causes back upstream.

## FAQ

**What is the difference between a claim rejection and a denial?**
A rejection means the claim was not accepted for processing, usually because of formatting or data errors caught by the clearinghouse or payer front end. A denial means the payer processed the claim and decided not to pay all or part of it. Rejections are corrected and resubmitted; denials are corrected, resubmitted or appealed.

**What are the most common causes of claim denials?**
Common categories include eligibility and coordination of benefits problems, non-covered services, missing prior authorization or referral, timely filing, coding errors and inaccurate patient demographics. In one 2025 vendor survey, billers most often cited coordination of benefits, non-coverage and prior authorization issues.

**How often should denials be worked?**
Daily or at least weekly, prioritized by dollar value and appeal deadline. Denials left for weeks risk missing appeal windows.

**What is a good denial rate?**
Benchmarks vary by specialty, payer mix and how the rate is calculated. Track your own denial rate by payer and reason each month and focus on the reasons you can prevent.

**Should denial work be in-house or outsourced?**
Either can work. What matters is that a specific person owns the queue, has payer knowledge and time to do it, and feeds root causes back to the front desk and coders.

# How to reduce AR days: a practical workflow and staffing guide

URL: https://medicalbillingteam.com/reduce-ar-days/

*Last reviewed: October 18, 2026.*

Days in accounts receivable (A/R) is the number most practice owners look at first, because it answers a simple question: how long does it take us to get paid? This guide explains how to measure it, the workflow that brings it down, and how to staff A/R follow-up so it actually happens. It's part of our [revenue cycle management staffing](/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/) series.

We won't promise a target number of days. Results depend on your specialty, payer mix and starting point. What we can describe is the process that consistently moves the number in the right direction.


## Step 1: Measure days in A/R the same way every month

A common formula:

1. Add your gross charges for the last 90 days (or 3 months).
2. Divide by 90 to get **average daily charges**.
3. Divide **current total A/R** by average daily charges.

Example: $900,000 in charges over 90 days = $10,000 per day. Total A/R of $400,000 ÷ $10,000 = 40 days in A/R. (Illustrative arithmetic only, not a benchmark.)

Track alongside it:

- **A/R by aging bucket:** 0-30, 31-60, 61-90, 91-120, 120+ days.
- **Percentage of A/R over 90 days** (or over 120).
- **A/R by payer**, so you can see which payers are slow.
- **Insurance vs patient A/R**, which need different workflows.

Credit balances, unposted payments and stale charges distort the number, so clean those up first. See our [RCM KPI definitions](/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/).


## Step 2: Get claims out fast and clean

You can't collect what you haven't billed.

- **Charge lag:** measure days from date of service to charge entry; aim to enter charges daily.
- **Claim scrubbing:** run edits before submission.
- **Rejections:** work clearinghouse and payer rejections every day. A rejected claim sitting for two weeks adds two weeks to A/R and inches toward timely filing limits. Medicare generally requires claims within one calendar year of the date of service ([CMS Claims Processing Manual, Ch. 1, §70](https://www.cms.gov/regulations-and-guidance/guidance/manuals/downloads/clm104c01.pdf)); many commercial payers allow less time.


## Step 3: Work A/R by priority, not by alphabet

A/R follow-up fails when staff start at the top of an alphabetical list every Monday. Instead:

1. **Sort by dollar value and age.** Work high-dollar claims in the 31-60 and 61-90 buckets first. They're old enough to need attention and young enough to fix.
2. **Group by payer.** One call or portal session can resolve several claims.
3. **Check status before calling.** Use payer portals and 276/277 claim status transactions where available.
4. **Act on what you find:** resubmit, send records, correct coding, bill secondary, or route to [denial management](/denial-management/).
5. **Set a follow-up date** for every claim touched and document the action.
6. **Escalate** claims stuck with a payer past its own processing commitments.


## Step 4: Fix the front-end causes

Much aging A/R starts at check-in. In a 2025 vendor survey, billers named coordination of benefits (45%), non-coverage (39%) and prior authorization or referral issues (31%) as top denial reasons, along with inaccurate demographics (25%) ([Tebra](https://www.tebra.com/theintake/getting-paid/medical-billing-pain-points-insights-solutions)). Each of these turns into aging A/R.

- Verify eligibility and benefits before every visit.
- Confirm authorizations and track visit limits and expiration dates.
- Capture insurance cards and demographics accurately at every visit.
- Collect copays and known patient balances at the time of service.

Our [eligibility verification and prior authorization guide](/eligibility-verification-prior-authorization/) covers this in detail.


## Step 5: Post payments accurately and promptly

Payment posting is where you discover underpayments, partial denials and secondary claims that need to go out. Post ERAs daily, reconcile to bank deposits, and flag:

- payments below contracted rates;
- zero-pay lines (these are denials);
- claims needing secondary or tertiary billing; and
- patient responsibility that should move to patient statements.


## Step 6: Handle patient A/R separately

Patient balances need statements, reminders, payment plans and clear communication, not payer calls. Keep the two workflows separate so neither gets neglected.


## Step 7: Clean up old A/R deliberately

For claims over 120 days:

- Check whether they can still be corrected or appealed within payer limits.
- Work the highest-value recoverable claims first.
- Write off only under your written policy, with documentation and approval.

Old A/R cleanup is often a short project that benefits from temporary extra hands.


## Staffing A/R follow-up

The most common reason A/R grows is simple: nobody has protected time to work it. Front-desk staff and office managers get pulled into phones and patients. Signs you need dedicated A/R capacity:

- A/R over 90 days is rising month over month.
- Claims are aging past timely filing or appeal limits.
- Follow-up happens in bursts, then stops.
- One person holds all the payer knowledge.

Options:

- **Add an in-house A/R specialist.** Good control; recruiting and turnover risk.
- **Outsource to a billing company.** Hands-off; less visibility.
- **Add a dedicated remote A/R specialist** who works your queue in your systems, under your rules. This is the model our operator provides.

A good A/R specialist knows payer portals, reads remittances fluently, documents every touch and escalates sensibly. Payer phone calls during US business hours matter, so confirm schedule overlap. Before granting any access, put a business associate agreement and access controls in place ([HIPAA guide](/hipaa-outsourced-medical-billing/)).


## What to report monthly

- Days in A/R (same method every month)
- A/R over 90 and over 120 days, in dollars and percent
- A/R by payer
- Claims touched per specialist per day and follow-up dates met
- Denials received and resolved
- Write-offs by reason

This site is operated by [Alliance Global Solutions](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/), which provides remote billing staff including A/R follow-up and [data entry support](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/virtual-assistant-skills/data-entry/). If you'd like a second opinion on your A/R workload, request a [free staffing assessment](/contact/) or use the [Medical Billing Health Checklist](/checklist/) to self-audit first.


## Common mistakes that keep A/R high

- **Working the oldest claims first, no matter what.** Very old, low-dollar claims may be past timely filing. Prioritize by dollar value and by what's still collectible.
- **Touching claims without a next step.** Every follow-up should end with a documented action and a date to check again.
- **Letting credits and unapplied payments sit.** They distort A/R reports and can create refund obligations.


## FAQ

**How do you calculate days in A/R?**
Total A/R divided by average daily charges (for example, last 90 days of charges ÷ 90). Use the same method monthly.

**What is a good number of days in A/R?**
It varies by specialty and payer mix. Track your own trend and your share of A/R over 90 days.

**What is the fastest way to reduce A/R days?**
Work high-dollar 31-90 day claims first, fix rejections daily, enter charges promptly and stop front-end errors.

**What does an AR follow-up specialist do?**
Works unpaid claims by age and value, checks status, calls payers, resubmits, routes denials and documents everything.

**Should old A/R be written off?**
Only under a written policy after documented efforts, and after checking whether claims can still be corrected or appealed.

## FAQ

**How do you calculate days in A/R?**
A common method divides total accounts receivable by average daily charges. For example, add gross charges for the last 90 days, divide by 90 to get average daily charges, then divide current total A/R by that number. Use the same method every month so the trend is meaningful.

**What is a good number of days in A/R?**
It varies by specialty, payer mix and calculation method, and many benchmark sources are member-only. Track your own trend and the share of A/R over 90 days, and compare with specialty data you trust.

**What is the fastest way to reduce A/R days?**
Work high-dollar claims in the 31-90 day buckets before they age further, fix rejections daily, submit charges promptly, and stop recurring front-end errors such as eligibility and authorization problems.

**What does an AR follow-up specialist do?**
They work unpaid and underpaid claims by age and value, check claim status in payer portals, call payers, correct and resubmit claims, route denials for appeal, and document every action.

**Should old A/R be written off?**
Only under a written write-off policy after documented collection efforts, and with approval. Before writing off, check whether claims can still be corrected or appealed within the payer's limits.

# Eligibility verification and prior authorization: workflows and staffing

URL: https://medicalbillingteam.com/eligibility-verification-prior-authorization/

*Last reviewed: October 18, 2026.*

Most denials are decided before the patient arrives. If coverage wasn't active, benefits weren't understood, or an authorization was missing, no amount of A/R follow-up will fully fix it. This guide covers eligibility verification and prior authorization, what changed recently in federal rules, the workflows that work, and how practices staff them. It's part of our [revenue cycle management staffing](/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/) series.


## Why the front end matters

In a 2025 vendor survey of billing professionals, the top denial reasons were coordination of benefits issues (45% of respondents), non-coverage (39%) and prior authorization or referral issues (31%) ([Tebra](https://www.tebra.com/theintake/getting-paid/medical-billing-pain-points-insights-solutions)). Federal transparency data show HealthCare.gov insurers attributed 9% of in-network claim denials in 2023 to lack of prior authorization or referral ([KFF](https://www.kff.org/private-insurance/claims-denials-and-appeals-in-aca-marketplace-plans-in-2023/)). All of these are front-end problems.


## Eligibility verification, step by step

### When to verify

- At scheduling, for new patients and new insurance.
- 24 to 72 hours before every visit, for everyone, since coverage changes.
- At check-in, by confirming card, ID and any changes.

### What to verify

- Active coverage on the date of service
- Plan type and network status for the rendering provider and location
- Copay, deductible (met and remaining), coinsurance, out-of-pocket maximum
- Coordination of benefits: is this plan primary?
- Service-specific limits (visit caps for therapy, for example)
- Referral and prior authorization requirements for the planned service

### How

Use real-time 270/271 eligibility transactions through your practice management system or clearinghouse where available, payer portals for detail, and phone calls when portals don't show what you need. Document what you found, where, and the reference number.

### What to do with the result

- Update demographics and insurance in the system.
- Flag inactive coverage and contact the patient before the visit.
- Give the front desk the patient's estimated responsibility so it can be collected at check-in.
- Trigger the authorization workflow if required.


## Verification of benefits (VOB) in behavioral health

Treatment centers and behavioral health programs often run a deeper VOB: benefits by level of care (detox, residential, partial hospitalization, intensive outpatient, outpatient), authorization and concurrent review requirements, out-of-network benefits and day limits. VOB staff usually work with admissions teams under time pressure. See our [behavioral health billing guide](/behavioral-health-billing/).


## Prior authorization, step by step

### The workload

The AMA's survey of 1,000 physicians found practices complete an average of 39 prior authorization requests per physician per week, spending about 13 hours on them, and that 40% of physicians have staff who work exclusively on prior authorizations ([AMA](https://www.ama-assn.org/practice-management/prior-authorization/fixing-prior-auth-nearly-40-prior-authorizations-week-way)).

### The workflow

1. **Identify** services needing authorization by payer and code, using payer lists. Keep a maintained matrix.
2. **Gather documentation:** orders, notes, prior treatments tried, test results.
3. **Submit** through the payer portal, electronic transaction or fax, as the payer requires.
4. **Track** pending requests daily, with a due date for each.
5. **Record** the authorization number, approved units or visits, and the date range in the practice management system so it flows to the claim.
6. **Monitor** expirations and visit counts, and request extensions before they run out.
7. **Handle denials:** request a peer-to-peer review if appropriate, or appeal with additional documentation.


## What changed: the CMS prior authorization rule

The CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization final rule (CMS-0057-F) applies to "impacted payers": Medicare Advantage organizations, state Medicaid and CHIP fee-for-service programs, Medicaid managed care plans, CHIP managed care entities and qualified health plan issuers on the federally facilitated exchanges ([CMS fact sheet](https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/cms-interoperability-and-prior-authorization-final-rule-cms-0057-f)). Key points from CMS:

- **Decision timeframes:** impacted payers, excluding FFE qualified health plans, must send prior authorization decisions within **72 hours** for expedited requests and **seven calendar days** for standard requests.
- **Specific denial reasons:** beginning in 2026, impacted payers must give a specific reason for denied prior authorization requests.
- **Public metrics:** payers must post certain prior authorization metrics annually.
- **Prior Authorization API:** payers must implement an API to support electronic requests and responses, generally by January 1, 2027.
- **Drugs are excluded** from these provisions.

For staff, this means more predictable turnaround from these payers and clearer denial reasons to work from, but the volume of authorizations doesn't go away. Commercial plans outside the rule follow their own contracts and applicable state laws.


## Measuring front-end performance

- Percentage of visits verified before the date of service
- Eligibility-related denials (count and dollars)
- Authorization-related denials
- Average days from authorization request to decision, by payer
- Visits performed without a valid authorization (should be zero)


## Staffing eligibility and prior authorization

Both jobs are detail-heavy, deadline-driven and largely done in portals and on the phone, which makes them a good fit for dedicated staff, local or remote. What matters:

- **Protected time.** Authorization work done "between patients" by front-desk staff tends to slip.
- **Payer knowledge.** A maintained authorization matrix and staff who know each payer's portal.
- **Schedule alignment.** Staff working ahead of your schedule (for example, verifying tomorrow's patients today) and overlapping payer phone hours.
- **Clear handoffs** with the front desk and clinicians for missing documentation.
- **Security.** Access only to scheduling, eligibility and authorization screens needed (minimum necessary), unique logins with MFA, and a signed BAA before access. See our [HIPAA guide](/hipaa-outsourced-medical-billing/).

This site is operated by [Alliance Global Solutions](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/), whose remote staff include eligibility, prior authorization and [administrative support](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/virtual-assistant-skills/administrative/) roles. If front-end work is backing up, request a [free staffing assessment](/contact/).


## Common front-end mistakes to avoid

- **Checking eligibility only for new patients.** Coverage changes at any time: job changes, plan renewals, Medicaid redeterminations. Re-verify before every visit, or at least whenever the schedule is built.
- **Stopping at "active coverage."** A plan can be active and still deny the service for lack of authorization, a visit limit, a carve-out or out-of-network status. Check benefits for the specific service.
- **Not recording the details.** Note who you spoke with, the reference number, the date and what was confirmed. If the payer later denies the claim, that record supports the appeal.
- **Losing track of expirations.** Authorizations expire and visit counts run out. Put both on a calendar with an owner and a lead time for renewal requests.
- **Treating the front desk as the only line of defense.** Front desk staff juggle phones, check-in and payments. A dedicated verification person or team, working a day or two ahead of the schedule, catches problems before the patient arrives.
- **Ignoring secondary coverage.** Coordination-of-benefits problems were the most commonly reported cause of rising denials in Tebra's 2025 survey of billers ([Tebra](https://www.tebra.com/theintake/getting-paid/medical-billing-pain-points-insights-solutions)). Ask every patient about other coverage and confirm which plan is primary.


## FAQ

**What is insurance eligibility verification?**
Confirming active coverage and benefits before a visit, including whether a referral or authorization is required.

**What is a VOB?**
Verification of benefits, a detailed benefits check common in behavioral health and treatment centers.

**How long do payers have to respond to prior authorization requests?**
For CMS-0057-F impacted payers (excluding FFE QHPs for this provision): 72 hours expedited, seven calendar days standard, from 2026.

**How much time do practices spend on prior authorization?**
AMA survey: 39 requests per physician per week, about 13 hours.

**Can eligibility and prior authorization be done by remote staff?**
Yes, with access to the right systems, clear rules and HIPAA safeguards.

## FAQ

**What is insurance eligibility verification?**
It is confirming, before a visit, that a patient's coverage is active and finding out benefits that affect payment: copay, deductible, coinsurance, plan type, network status, coordination of benefits, and whether a referral or prior authorization is required.

**What is a VOB?**
VOB stands for verification of benefits. The term is common in behavioral health and treatment centers, where staff verify detailed benefits for specific levels of care before admission.

**How long do payers have to respond to prior authorization requests?**
Under the CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization final rule, impacted payers such as Medicare Advantage and Medicaid managed care plans (excluding FFE qualified health plans for this provision) must send decisions within 72 hours for expedited requests and seven calendar days for standard requests, beginning in 2026. Commercial plans outside the rule follow their own contracts and state laws.

**How much time do practices spend on prior authorization?**
In an AMA survey of 1,000 physicians, practices reported an average of 39 prior authorization requests per physician per week, taking about 13 hours of physician and staff time.

**Can eligibility and prior authorization be done by remote staff?**
Yes. Both are largely portal- and phone-based, so remote staff can do them well with access to your scheduling system, payer portals and clear rules, plus HIPAA safeguards such as a BAA, MFA and role-based access.

# Hiring remote and offshore medical billers: what to look for

URL: https://medicalbillingteam.com/hire-remote-medical-billers/

*Last reviewed: October 18, 2026.*

Remote medical billers can add real capacity, or create new problems, depending on how you hire. This guide covers the roles you can fill, how to choose between a freelancer and an agency, what skills to test, the security practices to ask about, and how to onboard. It's written for practices and for billing companies adding staff. It's part of our [revenue cycle management staffing](/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/) series.


## Why practices and billing companies hire remotely

- **Hiring difficulty.** In a 2025 vendor survey, 38% of billing professionals said they struggle to find qualified candidates ([Tebra](https://www.tebra.com/theintake/getting-paid/medical-billing-pain-points-insights-solutions)).
- **Remote work is already normal in billing.** In the same survey, nearly 48% of respondents said they had implemented remote work arrangements ([Tebra](https://www.tebra.com/theintake/getting-paid/medical-billing-pain-points-insights-solutions)).
- **Coverage.** A second person who knows your payers keeps queues moving when someone is out.
- **Cost structure.** Remote and offshore staff can cost less per hour than local hires, but compare total cost, as our [cost guide](/medical-billing-staffing-cost/) explains.


## Roles you can hire remotely

- Billing / claims specialist
- A/R follow-up specialist
- Denial management specialist
- Eligibility and benefits verification (VOB) specialist
- Prior authorization coordinator
- Payment poster
- Medical coder (with credentials)
- Credentialing specialist
- Admissions / intake support (common in treatment centers)

Start with one well-defined queue. Eligibility, payment posting and A/R follow-up are common first roles because the work is measurable.


## Freelancer, agency or billing company?

| | Freelancer | Staffing agency | Billing company |
|---|---|---|---|
| Who directs the work | You | You | Vendor |
| Recruiting/vetting | You | Agency | Vendor |
| Backup coverage | Rarely | Usually (confirm) | Vendor |
| Equipment/security | Freelancer's own | Agency-managed (confirm) | Vendor |
| BAA | Must sign one | Agency signs | Vendor signs |
| Cost basis | Hourly | Monthly/hourly per FTE | % of collections or per claim |

Freelancers can work for small needs, but you carry the vetting, continuity and security risk. Agencies cost more than a freelancer's rate but handle employment, equipment, backfill and the business associate relationship. For general background on remote hiring, Alliance Global Solutions has published [tips on hiring a virtual assistant](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/how-to-hire-the-best-virtual-assistant-for-your-company/); billing roles need the extra steps below.


## Skills to look for

**Core billing skills**
- Experience in your practice management system, or a comparable one
- Payer portals and clearinghouse workflows
- Reading ERAs (835s) and EOBs; understanding CARC and RARC codes
- Claim status, corrected claims and appeals
- Timely filing awareness by payer

**Specialty knowledge** (if relevant)
- Behavioral health levels of care and authorizations ([behavioral health guide](/behavioral-health-billing/))
- Therapy visit limits and modifiers
- Lab or ASC billing rules

**Work habits**
- Clear written and spoken English for payer calls and internal notes
- Documentation of every action
- Comfort with queues, targets and follow-up dates
- Knowing when to escalate

**For coders:** recognized coding credentials and specialty experience, verified directly with the credentialing body.


## How to assess candidates

1. **Structured interview** with the same questions for every candidate.
2. **Practical test using fictional or de-identified data.** Never use real patient information in a test. Examples:
   - Interpret a sample remittance and identify denied lines and next steps.
   - Decide how to handle a coordination-of-benefits denial.
   - Write a payer call note.
   - Calculate days in A/R from sample numbers.
3. **Reference checks** on billing-specific work.
4. **Schedule check:** confirm hours overlap with payer phone lines and your team.

### Sample interview questions

- Walk me through how you work an A/R queue on a Monday morning.
- A claim was denied for no authorization, but you see one in the system. What do you do?
- How do you track timely filing limits across payers?
- What do you document after a payer call?
- Tell me about a time you found an underpayment.
- How do you handle a task you're not sure is within your authority?


## Security practices to ask about

Remote billers see protected health information all day. Before anyone logs in, ask the agency (or require of a freelancer):

- **Business associate agreement** signed before any PHI access ([HHS on business associates](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/guidance/business-associates/index.html))
- **Unique logins and multi-factor authentication** on every system
- **Secure remote access** via virtual desktop (VDI) or VPN
- **No local downloads, printing or USB storage**
- **Company-managed, encrypted devices** with current patches
- **Role-based, minimum necessary access**, reviewed regularly and removed the day someone leaves
- **HIPAA training** at onboarding and annually, with records
- **Background checks**
- **Current risk analysis** and incident response plan with a defined notification timeline
- **Work location controls:** office security or home-workspace privacy rules

And be wary of "HIPAA certified" claims. There is no official HIPAA certification; HHS's Office for Civil Rights doesn't certify vendors ([HHS](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/special-topics/health-information-technology/cloud-computing/index.html)). Our full [HIPAA guide](/hipaa-outsourced-medical-billing/) includes a 15-question checklist.

### Offshore-specific checks

- Confirm payer, Medicaid and government contracts don't restrict offshore access to member data.
- Know which legal entity signs the BAA and where it's based.
- Ask about power and internet redundancy.
- Include offshore access in your own HIPAA risk analysis.


## Onboarding: the first 30 days

**Week 1:** BAA and agreements signed; accounts created with role-based access and MFA; secure access tested; HIPAA and policy training; system walkthroughs.

**Week 2:** Shadow and practice on a limited queue; daily review of every action; payer-specific notes started.

**Week 3:** Own a defined queue with daily spot checks; agree on productivity and quality measures.

**Week 4:** Review results; adjust targets; document procedures the new person helped clarify; decide whether to expand scope.


## Managing remote billers well

- A daily or weekly check-in with clear priorities
- Shared queue reports so work is visible
- Written escalation rules (write-offs, refunds and appeals need approval)
- Monthly KPI review (see [RCM KPIs](/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/))
- Quick feedback on errors, so they're fixed once


## Next steps

This site is operated by [Alliance Global Solutions](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/), which places remote billing and RCM staff from the Philippines. To talk through roles, you can [reach the team directly](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/contact/) or request a [free staffing assessment](/contact/) here. Use the questions above with us, too.

A final tip: write down what "good" looks like before you hire, meaning the queues, volumes, quality checks and hours. A clear role description makes it easier to interview and onboard, and to judge whether the hire is working.



## FAQ

**Freelancer or agency?**
Freelancers suit small, simple needs; agencies handle vetting, employment, backfill and the BAA. Compare total cost and risk.

**What skills should a remote medical biller have?**
Practice management and portal experience, remittance reading, CARC/RARC codes, follow-up, clear English and documentation.

**How do I test a candidate?**
A practical test with fictional or de-identified data. Never real patient data.

**What security practices should I ask about?**
BAA, MFA, VDI/VPN, no downloads, managed devices, role-based access, training, background checks, risk analysis and incident response.

**Can offshore billers work US payer hours?**
Many do. Confirm the schedule in writing.

## FAQ

**Should I hire a freelance medical biller or go through an agency?**
A freelancer can work for small, simple needs but leaves you handling vetting, backup coverage, equipment and security. An agency typically handles recruiting, employment, equipment, backfill and HIPAA arrangements such as a BAA, but adds a margin. Compare total cost and risk, not just the hourly rate.

**What skills should a remote medical biller have?**
Experience with your practice management system or similar, payer portals, reading ERAs and EOBs, CARC/RARC codes, claim follow-up, clear written English and documentation habits. Specialty experience matters for behavioral health, therapy, labs and ASCs.

**How do I test a medical billing candidate?**
Use a short practical test with de-identified or fictional data: interpret a remittance, decide next steps on a denied claim, draft a payer call note, or calculate days in A/R from sample figures. Never use real patient data in a test.

**What security practices should I ask an agency about?**
A signed BAA, unique logins with MFA, secure remote access through VDI or VPN, no local downloads or printing, company-managed encrypted devices, role-based access, HIPAA training records, background checks, a current risk analysis and an incident response plan.

**Can offshore medical billers work US payer hours?**
Many offshore teams work schedules that overlap US business hours. Confirm the schedule in writing, because payer calls and same-day eligibility work depend on it.

# HIPAA and outsourced medical billing staff: what to check before anyone logs in

URL: https://medicalbillingteam.com/hipaa-outsourced-medical-billing/

*Last reviewed: October 18, 2026. General information, not legal advice. Talk to your own healthcare attorney or compliance adviser about your situation.*

Billing work runs on patient data. Names, dates of birth, member IDs, diagnosis and procedure codes and payment details all sit on the screens your billing staff use every day. So when you bring in outsourced, remote or offshore billing staff through an agency, HIPAA is not a box to tick at the end. It shapes which agency you choose, how the contract is written, how access is set up and what happens if something goes wrong.

This guide explains the main HIPAA concepts that apply when a staffing agency provides dedicated billing staff, and ends with a checklist of questions to ask any agency, including ours.


## First, a myth: there is no "HIPAA certification"

You will see agencies and freelancers describe themselves as "HIPAA certified." There is no such official credential. The HHS Office for Civil Rights (OCR), which enforces HIPAA, says plainly that it "does not endorse, certify, or recommend specific technology or products" ([HHS, Guidance on HIPAA & Cloud Computing](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/special-topics/health-information-technology/cloud-computing/index.html)). Training companies issue certificates of course completion, and independent auditors can assess security programs, but neither is a government HIPAA certification.

What matters is evidence of specific safeguards: a signed business associate agreement, documented policies, training records, a current risk analysis and technical controls you can verify. We don't claim to be "HIPAA certified," and you shouldn't accept that claim from anyone.


## Why an agency is usually a business associate

HIPAA's rules apply directly to **covered entities** (health plans, clearinghouses and health care providers that conduct standard electronic transactions such as claims) and to their **business associates**. HHS defines a business associate generally as a person or organization, other than a member of the covered entity's workforce, that performs functions or services on behalf of a covered entity involving the use or disclosure of protected health information (PHI). HHS lists **billing, claims processing and practice management** among the examples ([HHS, Business Associates](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/guidance/business-associates/index.html)).

A staffing agency whose people work your claims, check eligibility or post payments in your systems is therefore typically a business associate. A billing company that serves practices is often itself a business associate, so if it adds agency staff, the agency becomes a **subcontractor business associate**, and HHS says a business associate must have a BAA with its subcontractor before disclosing PHI to it ([HHS](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/guidance/business-associates/index.html)).

Business associates are not just contractually bound. Since the HITECH Act, they are directly liable for complying with the Security Rule's safeguards and certain Privacy Rule provisions ([HHS, Summary of the Security Rule](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/security/laws-regulations/index.html)).


## The business associate agreement (BAA)

HIPAA permits you to share PHI with a business associate only after you obtain "satisfactory assurances," in the form of a BAA, that it will safeguard the information ([HHS](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/guidance/business-associates/index.html)). According to HHS, a BAA must, among other things:

- describe the permitted and required uses and disclosures of PHI;
- state that the business associate will not use or further disclose PHI except as the agreement permits or the law requires;
- require compliance with applicable Security Rule requirements;
- require reporting of security incidents and breaches of unsecured PHI;
- require that subcontractors agree to the same restrictions through their own BAAs; and
- address return or destruction of PHI at the end of the relationship, where feasible.

HHS publishes [sample business associate agreement provisions](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/covered-entities/sample-business-associate-agreement-provisions/index.html). Have your counsel review any BAA rather than relying on the agency's template alone.

**Practical tip:** sign the BAA before you create a single login. No PHI should move during interviews or trials without one.


## PHI handling and the "minimum necessary" standard

The Privacy Rule asks covered entities and business associates to make reasonable efforts to use, disclose and request only the **minimum necessary** PHI for the purpose, and to restrict workforce access based on role ([HHS, Summary of the Privacy Rule](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/laws-regulations/index.html)). For billing teams, minimum necessary in practice looks like:

- A payment poster gets posting screens and remittance files, not full clinical charts.
- An A/R follow-up specialist sees the claims and payer correspondence in their queue, not every patient in the system.
- An eligibility specialist uses payer portals and scheduling data, not visit notes.
- PHI is never pasted into personal email, chat apps, unapproved AI tools or spreadsheets on personal drives.

Behavioral health and substance use disorder programs carry extra rules. Records covered by 42 CFR Part 2 have their own consent and redisclosure limits; HHS notes that compliance with the 2024 Part 2 final rule was required by February 16, 2026 ([HHS, Part 2](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/special-topics/hipaa-part-2/index.html)). See our [behavioral health billing guide](/behavioral-health-billing/).


## Access controls to expect

The Security Rule is "technology neutral." It requires access control, audit controls, integrity controls, person or entity authentication and transmission security, but lets each organization choose reasonable and appropriate measures based on its risks ([HHS](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/security/laws-regulations/index.html)). For remote and offshore billing staff, these are common, sensible controls to ask about:

- **Unique user IDs.** No shared logins, ever. Each person's activity should be traceable.
- **Multi-factor authentication (MFA)** on your practice management system, clearinghouse, payer portals, email and the agency's own systems.
- **Secure remote access.** A VPN, or better, a virtual desktop (VDI) so PHI stays on your servers or cloud and is only displayed remotely.
- **No local downloads, printing or USB storage.** Endpoint controls that block saving files, screenshots where feasible, and removable media.
- **Role-based access** mapped to each job, reviewed regularly, and removed the same day someone leaves.
- **Managed, encrypted company devices** with current patches and endpoint protection, rather than personal computers.
- **Activity logging and audit review.** Logs of who accessed what and when, reviewed on a schedule.
- **Physical controls.** For office-based teams, controlled facility access and clean-desk rules; for home-based staff, private workspaces and screen-privacy rules.


## Workforce training

The Security Rule requires security awareness training for all workforce members and appropriate sanctions for people who violate policies ([HHS](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/security/laws-regulations/index.html)). Ask the agency for:

- HIPAA privacy and security training at onboarding and at least annually;
- phishing and social-engineering awareness;
- client-specific training on your policies, payer portals and escalation paths;
- signed confidentiality agreements; and
- training records you can review.


## Audits and risk assessments

Both covered entities and business associates must perform an accurate and thorough **risk analysis** of threats to electronic PHI, manage those risks, and periodically evaluate their safeguards ([HHS, Security Rule summary](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/security/laws-regulations/index.html)). When you add an agency:

- Update your own risk analysis to include the new remote access paths and locations.
- Ask when the agency last completed its risk analysis and what it changed as a result.
- Ask whether it has had an independent security assessment (for example, a third-party audit or penetration test) and whether it will share a summary.
- Agree in writing on your right to request documentation. HHS notes that HIPAA does not expressly require vendors to allow customer audits, but customers may require additional assurances through the BAA or service agreement ([HHS, Cloud Computing FAQ 10](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/special-topics/health-information-technology/cloud-computing/index.html)).


## Breach notification

Under the Breach Notification Rule, if a breach of unsecured PHI occurs at or by a business associate, the business associate must notify the covered entity **without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 days** after discovery, and provide, to the extent possible, the identity of affected individuals ([HHS, Breach Notification Rule](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/breach-notification/index.html)). The covered entity then has its own obligations to notify individuals, HHS and, for larger breaches, the media.

Many practices negotiate a much shorter reporting window in the BAA. Ask the agency to walk you through its incident response plan: who detects an incident, who calls you, and how fast.


## Offshore considerations

HIPAA does not prohibit offshore work. In its cloud guidance, HHS says the HIPAA Rules "do not include requirements specific to protection of electronic protected health information (ePHI) processed or stored by a CSP or any other business associate outside of the United States," but warns that overseas outsourcing "may increase the risks and vulnerabilities to the information or present special considerations with respect to enforceability" ([HHS, Cloud Computing FAQ 9](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/special-topics/health-information-technology/cloud-computing/index.html)). Practical steps:

- **Keep PHI onshore where possible.** With VDI, data stays in your US-hosted systems and offshore staff only view it.
- **Know the legal entity.** Confirm which company signs the BAA, where it is incorporated, and whether a US entity is accountable.
- **Check payer and state rules.** Some payer contracts, Medicaid programs and government plans restrict offshore access to member data. Check before you assign offshore staff to those accounts.
- **Plan for continuity.** Ask about power, internet redundancy and backup work sites.
- **Document it in your risk analysis**, including country-specific risks.


## Questions to ask any billing staffing agency

Print this list and use it on every agency call, including with us.

1. Will you sign our BAA (or offer one our counsel can review) before any access to PHI?
2. Which legal entity signs, and do you use any subcontractors who would touch PHI? Do they sign BAAs too?
3. When did you last complete a HIPAA security risk analysis? What changed afterward?
4. Have you had an independent security assessment? Can you share a summary?
5. Do your staff use unique logins and MFA on every system?
6. Do staff work through VDI or VPN? Can they download, print, screenshot or use USB storage?
7. Are devices company-managed and encrypted? Who patches them?
8. How do you enforce minimum necessary and role-based access?
9. What background checks do you run on staff?
10. What HIPAA training do staff complete, how often, and can we see records?
11. Do staff work from an office, from home, or both? What physical safeguards apply?
12. What is your incident response plan, and how fast will you notify us of a suspected incident?
13. How do you remove access on the day someone leaves?
14. How do you handle Part 2 records, if we have them?
15. Do you claim to be "HIPAA certified"? (The right answer is that no such official certification exists.)


## How this site handles your information

Our forms never ask for patient information, and we ask you not to submit any. We collect only business contact and practice-level details. See our [Privacy Policy](/privacy/).


## Next steps

- Compare options in our [medical billing staffing cost guide](/medical-billing-staffing-cost/).
- Read [how to hire remote and offshore medical billers](/hire-remote-medical-billers/).
- Ask us these questions directly with a [free staffing assessment](/contact/). This site is operated by [Alliance Global Solutions](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/about-us/); you can also reach the company through its [contact page](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/contact/).


## FAQ

**Is there such a thing as HIPAA certification?**
No. There is no official HIPAA certification for companies or people. OCR does not endorse or certify products or vendors.

**Does a billing staffing agency need to sign a BAA?**
If its staff will create, receive, maintain or transmit PHI on your behalf, it is generally a business associate and a BAA is required before PHI is shared.

**Can offshore staff access PHI under HIPAA?**
HIPAA has no offshore-specific ban, but HHS notes increased risk and enforceability concerns. Address them in your risk analysis and safeguards, and check payer contracts.

**How quickly must a business associate report a breach?**
Without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 days after discovery. Many BAAs require faster notice.

**What does minimum necessary mean for billing staff?**
Access only to the PHI each role needs, enforced by role-based permissions.

## FAQ

**Is there such a thing as HIPAA certification?**
No. There is no official HIPAA certification for companies or individuals. HHS's Office for Civil Rights says it does not endorse, certify or recommend specific technology or products. Private training courses may issue certificates, but these are not government certification of HIPAA compliance.

**Does a medical billing staffing agency need to sign a BAA?**
If the agency or its staff will create, receive, maintain or transmit protected health information on your behalf, such as by working claims in your billing system, the agency is generally a business associate and HIPAA requires a business associate agreement before PHI is shared. Confirm your situation with your own counsel.

**Can offshore staff access PHI under HIPAA?**
HIPAA does not ban offshore work. HHS guidance on cloud services says the rules do not include requirements specific to PHI handled outside the US, but notes that overseas arrangements may increase risk and raise enforceability concerns. Those risks should be addressed in your risk analysis and safeguards.

**How quickly must a business associate report a breach?**
Under the Breach Notification Rule, a business associate must notify the covered entity without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 days after discovering a breach of unsecured PHI. Many BAAs set a shorter deadline.

**What does minimum necessary mean for billing staff?**
It means making reasonable efforts to use, disclose and request only the minimum PHI needed for the task. For billing staff, that usually means role-based access limited to the queues, screens and payers they actually work.
